text: A song of ascents. Of Solomon. Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain. Unless the LORD watches over the city, the watchman keeps guard in vain.
In vain you rise early and stay up late, eating the bread of anxious toil; for the LORD gives sleep to the one he loves.

versions.text: In vain you rise early and stay up late, eating the bread of toil— for he gives sleep to the one he loves.
versions.explanation: Two small improvements for accuracy and oral clarity: (1) הָעֲצָבִים carries the sense of painful, anxious labor, so "bread of anxious toil" renders it more fully than "bread of toil"; (2) the subject of יִתֵּן is unnamed in this verse, and for a listener "he" can be misheard as referring to the person who rises early, so naming the LORD (carried over from v.1) removes the ambiguity. A semicolon also reads more smoothly aloud than the dash.

text: Look, children are a heritage from the LORD; the fruit of the womb is a reward.

versions.text: Children are indeed the LORD's inheritance; the fruit of the womb is his reward.
versions.explanation: The construct phrase נַחֲלַת יְהוָה means a heritage/inheritance given BY the LORD, not something the LORD inherits. "The LORD's inheritance" and "his reward" reverse the sense, making God the recipient rather than the giver. Also הִנֵּה is a presentative particle better rendered as "Look" or "Behold" than as the adverb "indeed."

text: Like arrows in the hand of a warrior, so are the sons of one's youth.

versions.text: Like arrows in the hand of a warrior are the sons born in one's youth.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has the correlative כְּ...כֵּן ("like... so"), which the current rendering flattens. "Born in one's youth" also adds an interpretive element not present in the simple construct בְּנֵי הַנְּעוּרִים ("sons of youth"); the shorter phrase keeps the parallel rhythm for reading aloud.

text: How blessed is the man whose quiver is full of them! They will not be put to shame when they contend with enemies at the gate.

versions.text: Blessed is the man whose quiver is full of them. He will not be put to shame when he confronts his enemies at the gate.
versions.explanation: Both verbs (יֵבֹשׁוּ, יְדַבְּרוּ) are plural, referring to the sons/arrows, not to the father in the singular. The translation should keep the plural subject. Also "enemies" has no possessive suffix in Hebrew, and the idiom יְדַבְּרוּ אֶת means to contend or plead a case at the gate (the place of judgment).
